extraction_notes.note: Section 3.1 re-introduces $L_-$ and $L_+$ (footnote) after DP12 already defined them; treated as a repeated definition (also_stated_at), so the checker's 'introduced symbol with no definition node' warning for $L_\pm$ remains.
The paper reuses ${\mathcal L}_h$ and $\sigma_0$ for different operators/quantities in Section 4 and Appendix A; no term edges drawn from DP15/DP20 where the symbol is used in the other sense.

Section 4 has no proof environment but is entirely the proof of Theorem 2 (ends 'This is exactly the statement of Theorem 105 and the proof is completed'); extracted as one section-filling proof with each subsection a step.
Subsection 3.2 is a prose proof of Theorem 1; it builds on the informal analysis of 3.1, whose numbered equations are kept as standalone equation nodes rather than as a proof.
Appendix A is a computation of the translational eigenvalue that the paper calls inconclusive; kept as a remark (self-contained aside) rather than a claim.
The explicit cnoidal solution (1.5)-(1.6) is stated in prose and attributed to Barashenkov-Smirnov and Matsko et al. in the next sentence; made an external theorem rather than a claim.

The signs in (ant1) and (ant4) are established from plotted figures and a Mathematica evaluation, so Proposition 7 is marked rigor numerical; the proof also reuses alpha as the dn-wave amplitude, clashing with the detuning parameter.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement:
Let $\varphi_{\alpha}=\varphi_{\alpha, 1}+i\varphi_{\alpha, 2}$ be  a solution of \eqref{110}. Then, we have
	\begin{equation} \left| \begin{array}{ll} \varphi_{\alpha,1}^{''}-\varphi_{\alpha,1}+2(\varphi_{\alpha,1}^2+\varphi_{\alpha, 2}^2)\varphi_{\alpha, 1}-\alpha\varphi_{\alpha, 2}=0 \\
	\\
	\varphi_{\alpha,2}^{''}-\varphi_{\alpha,2}+2(\varphi_{\alpha,1}^2+\varphi_{\alpha, 2}^2)\varphi_{\alpha, 2}+\alpha\varphi_{\alpha, 1}=0.
	\end{array} \right.
	\end{equation}
	Denoting the second order self-adjoint differential operator $L:=-\partial_x^2+1 - 2(\varphi_{\alpha,1}^2+\varphi_{\alpha, 2}^2)$, we see that \eqref{120} is a relationship in the form
	$$
	\left| \begin{array}{l}
	L[\varphi_{\alpha,1}]=-\alpha \varphi_{\alpha,2} \\
	L[\varphi_{\alpha,2}]=\alpha \varphi_{\alpha,1}.
	\end{array}
	\right.
	$$
	Thus, applying $L$ to to first equation, we obtain $L^2[\varphi_{\alpha,1}]=-\alpha^2 \varphi_{\alpha,1}$. By taking a dot product with $\varphi_{\alpha,1}$, we obtain
	$$
	0\leq \|L \varphi_{\alpha,1}\|^2=\dpr{L^2[\varphi_{\alpha,1}]}{\varphi_{\alpha,1}}=-\alpha^2\|\varphi_{\alpha,1}\|^2<0,
	$$
	which  is a contradiction.

nodes.statement:
The solution of   (\ref{1.4}) is given by
 \begin{equation} \varphi(x)=\frac{\zeta_4(\zeta_3-\zeta_1)+\zeta_1(\zeta_4-\zeta_3)sn^2(\frac{x}{\sqrt{g}}, \kappa)}{(\zeta_3-\zeta_1)+(\zeta_4-\zeta_3)sn^2(\frac{x}{\sqrt{g}}, \kappa)},

\end{array} \right.
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3
nodes.statement:
Take a dot product with $\varphi=\varphi_1+i \varphi_2$ in \eqref{1.15}. Then, since its left-hand side is real, taking imaginary parts results in
  $$
  \alpha \|\varphi\|^2 = h \int_{-T}^T  \varphi_2(x) dx\leq h \sqrt{2 T} \|\varphi\|
  $$
  This implies that $\alpha=O(h)$.

nodes.name: Existence of O(1) Kerr combs for small h and alpha
nodes.statement:
Let $\alpha_0$ is such that $ 0<\alpha_0<\f{\dpr{1}{\varphi_0}}{\|\varphi_0\|^2}$. Then, there exists $h_0=h_0(\alpha_0)>0$, so that for every $h: 0<h<h_0$ and $\alpha:=\alpha_0 h$, there exists a stationary solution $\varphi_{\alpha}=\varphi_{\alpha,1}+i \varphi_{\alpha,2}$ of
  	\eqref{1.1}  or equivalently  solutions $\varphi_{\alpha,1}(h), \varphi_{\alpha,2}(h)$ of the profile system   \eqref{150}. Moreover, there is the following Taylor expansions formula for the coefficients
  	\begin{eqnarray} \varphi_{\alpha,1} &=& (a_0+\f{b_0}{2} h D_2^0+O(h^2))  \varphi_0+h \Psi_1^0 +O_{\{\varphi_0\}^\perp}(h^2)\\ \varphi_{\alpha,2} &=&  (b_0-\f{a_0}{2} h D_2^0+O(h^2))  \varphi_0+h \Psi_2^0 +O_{\{\varphi_0\}^\perp}(h^2)
  	\end{eqnarray}
  	where
  	\begin{eqnarray*}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4
nodes.statement:
Note that $\varphi_0$ satisfies \eqref{1.1} with $h=0$, hence ${\mathcal L}_{-,0}[\varphi_0]=0$. Since $\varphi_0>0$, it follows
 by Sturm-Liouville theory that ${\mathcal L}_{-,0}\geq 0$ and $0$ is the bottom of the spectrum and
 ${\mathcal L}_{-,0}|_{\{\varphi_0\}^\perp}>0$.

 Next, we show the properties of ${\mathcal L}_{+,0}$. First, observe that the function $\varphi_0$ can be realized as a (rescaled)
 minimizer of the following constrained minimization problem
 \begin{equation} \left\{
 \begin{array}{l}
 \int_{-T}^T [(\varphi'(x))^2 - \varphi^4(x)] dx\to \min \\
 \int_{-T}^T \varphi^2(x) dx=1
 \end{array}
 \right.
 \end{equation}
 Indeed, the existence of a minimizer of \eqref{30} is standard, moreover such minimizer is necessarily
  bell-shaped. Its Euler-Lagrange equation is in the form
\begin{equation} \varphi''- 2 \varphi^3 = -\sigma \varphi,
\end{equation}
which has an unique (bell-shaped) solution, namely a rescaled version of $\varphi_0$.
As a consequence of this, it is standard to show that $n({\mathcal L}_{+,0})=1$, since $\dpr{{\mathcal L}_{+,0} \varphi_0}{\varphi_0}<0$ and as a consequence of the minimization properties of $\varphi_0$,
${\mathcal L}_{+,0}|_{\{\varphi_0\}^\perp}\geq 0$. Also, by a direct differentiation of the profile equation \eqref{1.1} (with $h=0$), we conclude ${\mathcal L}_{+,0}[\varphi'_0]=0$.

Finally, let us show that $Ker[{\mathcal L}_{+,0}]=span\{\varphi_0'\}$. In order to do that, we will show that the  second independent solution of the equation  ${\mathcal L}_{+,0}[g]=0$ does not belong to the space $L^2_{per.}[-T,T]$. Normally,
 such a solution $g$ can be written down by the reduction of order   formula as follows
$$
g(x)=\varphi'_0(x)\int_{a}^x \f{1}{(\varphi'_0(y))^2} dy
$$
The problem is that such a formula blows up whenever the interval of integration contains $0$. So, we use an alternative description of the eigenfunction, due to Rofe-Beketov, (see \cite{Teschl},  Exercise 5.11, p. 154)
$$
g(x)=\varphi_0'(x) \int_0^x \f{(2-6\varphi_0^2(y))((\varphi_0'(y))^2-(\varphi_0''(y))^2)}{((\varphi_0'(y))^2+(\varphi_0''(y))^2))^2} dy -
\f{\varphi_0''(x)}{(\varphi_0'(x))^2+(\varphi_0''(x))^2}
$$
This function is well-defined and satisfies ${\mathcal L}_{+,0}[g]=0$. In order to show that the eigenvalue at zero is simple, it suffices to prove that $g$ is not $2T$ periodic. Clearly, the second part of the formula in $g$ is $2T$ periodic, so we concentrate on showing that the first piece, $g_1(x)$  is non-periodic. In fact, $g_1(-T)=g_1(T)$, since $\varphi_0'(T)=\varphi'_0(-T)=0$.

We show that in fact $g_1'(-T)\neq g_1'(T)$. Since, $\varphi_0''(-T)=\varphi_0''(T)\neq 0$, it suffices to show that
$$
\int_0^T \f{(2-6\varphi_0^2(y))((\varphi_0'(y))^2-(\varphi_0''(y))^2)}{((\varphi_0'(y))^2+(\varphi_0''(y))^2))^2} dy\neq \int_0^{-T} \f{(2-6\varphi_0^2(y))((\varphi_0'(y))^2-(\varphi_0''(y))^2)}{((\varphi_0'(y))^2+(\varphi_0''(y))^2))^2} dy.
$$
Since the integrand is even, this is equivalent to
\begin{equation} \int_0^T \f{(2-6\varphi_0^2(y))((\varphi_0'(y))^2-(\varphi_0''(y))^2)}{((\varphi_0'(y))^2+(\varphi_0''(y))^2))^2} dy\neq 0.
\end{equation}
We postpone the verification of \eqref{posle} and the proofs of $\dpr{{\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1} \varphi_0}{\varphi_0}<0$
and $\dpr{{\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1} \varphi_0}{1}=0$ for the appendix.  The computations are somewhat  long and technical, but otherwise standard.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement:
By differentiating with respect to $h$ the profile equation, we obtain ${\mathcal L}_{+,h}[\partial_h \varphi_h]=1$. As a consequence, since we know $Ker[{\mathcal L}_{+,h}]=span[\varphi'_h]$ (and hence $1\perp Ker[{\mathcal L}_{+,h}]$),
 $$
 \partial_h\varphi_h={\mathcal L}_{+,h}^{-1}[1]+\delta \varphi_h',
 $$
 for some $\delta$. We claim $\delta=0$. Indeed, we know that $\varphi_h$ is an even function, and so is $\partial_h \varphi_h$. Clearly ${\mathcal L}_{+,h}$ (and its inverse on $Ker[{\mathcal L}_{+,h}]^\perp$)  acts invariantly on the even subspace, so ${\mathcal L}_{+,h}^{-1}[1]$ is even as well. Thus, the odd piece $\delta \varphi_h'$ is actually zero, whence  $\delta=0$. Thus,
 \begin{equation} \varphi_h=\varphi_0+h {\mathcal L}_{+,h}^{-1}[1]+O(h^2).
 \end{equation}
 Next, since ${\mathcal L}_{-,0}$ has a simple eigenvalue at zero, $L_{-,h}$ has a single eigenvalue close to zero,
 in the form $\lambda_0({\mathcal L}_{-,h})=a h+O(h^2)$. Say the corresponding eigenfunction is in the form $\varphi_0+ h z$,
 $z\in H^2[-T,T]$. Thus,
\begin{equation} {\mathcal L}_{-,h}[\varphi_0+ h z]=a h(\varphi_0+ h z).
\end{equation}
 However, by \eqref{35},
\begin{eqnarray*}
{\mathcal L}_{-,h} &=&-\partial_x^2+1-2\varphi_h^2=-\partial_x^2+1-2 \varphi_0^2 - 4 h  {\mathcal L}_{+,h}^{-1}[1] \varphi^0  +O(h^2)= \\
&=&{\mathcal L}_{-,0} - 4 h \varphi_0   {\mathcal L}_{+,h}^{-1}[1] +O(h^2).
\end{eqnarray*}
By taking the first order in $h$ terms in \eqref{40}, we obtain
$$
 {\mathcal L}_{-,0} z =4 \varphi_0^2  {\mathcal L}_{+,h}^{-1}[1] +a \varphi_0.
$$
 Now, take dot product with $\varphi_0$. Note that since $1\perp Ker[{\mathcal L}_{+,h}]$, we have that \\  ${\mathcal L}_{+,h}^{-1}[1]={\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1}[1]+O(h)$. Since $\dpr{{\mathcal L}_{-,0} z }{\varphi_0}= \dpr{ z }{{\mathcal L}_{-,0}[\varphi_0]}=0$,
we obtain the relation
$$
a\|\varphi_0\|^2+4 \dpr{\varphi_0^3}{{\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1}[1]}=0.
$$
Thus,
$
a=-\f{4}{\|\varphi_0\|^2} \dpr{{\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1}[\varphi_0^3]}{1}.
$
However,  the profile equation can be rewritten as  $${\mathcal L}_{+,0}[\varphi_0]=-4 \varphi_0^3,$$
whence ${\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1}[\varphi_0^3]=-\f{1}{4} \varphi_0+\delta \varphi_0'$ and
$$
a= \f{\int_{-T}^{T} \varphi_0(x)dx}{\int_{-T}^{T} \varphi_0^2 (x)dx}>0.
$$
Also,
$$
z={\mathcal L}_{-,0}^{-1}\left[4 \varphi_0^2  {\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1}[1] + \f{\int_{-T}^{T} \varphi_0(x)dx}{\int_{-T}^{T} \varphi_0^2 (x)dx}  \varphi_0 \right]+O(h),
$$
which is \eqref{28}.

nodes.name: Claim delta=0

nodes.name: Derivation of Proposition 5
nodes.statement:
To this end,  for the spectral analysis of \eqref{24}, we are  looking to find the pair $\lambda=0, \vec{v}=\left(\begin{array}{ll} 0\\ \varphi_0 \end{array} \right)$, which solves \eqref{24} for $h=0$.  In other words, we claim that the instability established in Proposition \ref{prop:10} is due to the bifurcation of the zero eigenvalue\footnote{present at $h=0$, corresponding to modulational invariance, which comes with algebraic multiplicity two} onto the real line - one positive and one negative.
 Multiplying  \eqref{24}by ${\mathcal J}$ and taking the ansatz $v_2=\varphi_h+h z, z\in L^2_{even}[-T,T]$ (and observing that   ${\mathcal L}_{+,h}$ is invertible on the even subspace), we obtain
 \begin{equation} {\mathcal L}_{-,h}[\varphi_h+ h z]=-\lambda^2 {\mathcal L}_{+,h}^{-1}[\varphi_h+h z].
 \end{equation}
 Taking into account ${\mathcal L}_{-,h}[\varphi_h]=h$ and ${\mathcal L}_{+,h}^{-1}[\varphi_h]={\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1}[\varphi_0]+O(h)$,
  we arrive at
  \begin{equation} h(1+{\mathcal L}_{-,h}[z])=-\lambda^2[{\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1}[\varphi_0]+F(h,z)], \ \ F(h,z)=O(h)+O(z).
  \end{equation}
 It becomes clear that the ansatz for the eigenvalue $\lambda$ must be in the form $\lambda=a\sqrt{h}+O(h)$, whence by taking dot product of \eqref{70} with $\varphi_h$, and taking only $O(h)$ terms
 $$
 -a^2 \dpr{{\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1} \varphi_0} {\varphi_0}=\int_{-T}^T  \varphi_0(x) dx.
 $$
 Recalling $\dpr{{\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1} \varphi_0} {\varphi_0}<0$, this yields the formula
 $$
 a=\sqrt{\f{\int_{-T}^T  \varphi_0(x) dx}{-\dpr{{\mathcal L}_{+,0}^{-1} \varphi_0} {\varphi_0}}}>0.
 $$
 Furthermore, \eqref{70} is solvable for small $h$, by the inverse function theorem. In this way, we have shown the following, more precise and quantitative version of Proposition \ref{prop:10}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1 (rigorous construction)
nodes.statement:
We now setup the full non-linear problem \eqref{151}, with $0<h<<1$, in the equivalent formulation \eqref{190}. More precisely, armed with the results from our informal analysis, we  set the unknown function \\  $q=\varphi_{\alpha,1}-\varphi_{\alpha,2}+i(\varphi_{\alpha,1}+\varphi_{\alpha,2}) \in L^2_{per.}[-T,T]$ in the form
 $$
 q=(c+d h)\varphi_0+ h \Psi, \Psi\perp \varphi_0
 $$
 where
 $$
 c=a_0-b_0+i(a_0+b_0),
 $$
  and $a_0, b_0$ are given by \eqref{180}, \eqref{185} and \eqref{211}), in terms of $\alpha_0$. Note that $|c|^2=2$. Also, in accordance with \eqref{211}, we require $\alpha_0: 0<\alpha_0 < \f{\dpr{1}{\varphi_0}}{\|\varphi_0\|^2}$.

Now that we have set $q$ (and in particular $a_0, b_0$), we are looking for a scalar function $d=d(h)$ and a function $\Psi(h)\in \{\varphi_0\}^\perp$, so that \eqref{190} holds. We compute
$$
|q|^2=2\varphi_0^2 +h V+h^2[|d|^2\varphi_0^2+\varphi_0(d \bar{\Psi}+\bar{d} \Psi) +|\Psi|^2],
$$
 where
 $$
 V= 2  \varphi_0^2 \Re[c\bar{d}]+2 \varphi_0\Re[c \bar{\Psi}]
 $$
  is a real-valued function as
  before. Introduce the {\it real-valued function}
 $$
 G=G(d, \Psi)=|d|^2\varphi_0^2+\varphi_0(d \bar{\Psi}+\bar{d} \Psi) +|\Psi|^2.
 $$
 We thus have a formula for $\tilde{{\mathcal L}}$ as follows
 $$
 \tilde{{\mathcal L}}=-\partial_x^2+1- |q|^2= -\partial_x^2+1-2\varphi_0^2 - h V - h^2 G=L_- - h V -h^2 G.
 $$
 Plugging this in \eqref{190}, we obtain the following relation
 \begin{equation} (L_- - h(V+i\alpha_0)-h^2 G)[(c+d h)\varphi_0+h \Psi]=h(1+i).
 \end{equation}
 After some algebraic manipulations,  we obtain
  \begin{equation} L_- \Psi-c(V+i \alpha_0)\varphi_0-(1+i)-h[(V+i\alpha_0)(d \varphi_0 +\Psi)+c \varphi_0 G]=h^2 G(d, \Psi)\Psi.
  \end{equation}
 Similar to the derivation of \eqref{210}, we take \eqref{310} and its complex conjugate to obtain the following {\it non-linear} in $h$ system of equations
  \begin{eqnarray*}
  & & \left(\begin{array}{cc}
  -\partial_x^2+1- 4\varphi_0^2 & -c^2 \varphi_0^2 \\
  -\bar{c}^2 \varphi_0^2 & -\partial_x^2+1- 4\varphi_0^2
  \end{array}\right) \left(\begin{array}{c}
  \Psi \\ \bar{\Psi}
  \end{array}\right) =  \left(\begin{array}{c}
  1+i +i \alpha_0 c \varphi_0 +2 \varphi_0^3 c   \Re[c\bar{d}] \\  1-i -i \alpha_0 \bar{c} \varphi_0 + 2 \varphi_0^3 \bar{c}   \Re[c\bar{d}]
  \end{array}\right)+ \\
  &+& h \left(\begin{array}{c}
  	 (V+i\alpha_0)(d\varphi_0 +\Psi)+c \varphi_0 G \\
  	 (V-i\alpha_0)(\bar{d} \varphi_0 +\bar{\Psi})+\bar{c}\varphi_0 G
  \end{array}\right)+h^2 \left(\begin{array}{c}
   G(d, \Psi)\Psi \\G(d, \Psi)\bar{\Psi}
\end{array}\right)
  \end{eqnarray*}
 Diagonalizing yields the equivalent equations
  \begin{eqnarray} L_+[\bar{c}\Psi+c\bar{\Psi}] &=&  4a_0 +8 \varphi_0^3  \Re[c\bar{d}]+h E_1(h,d,\Psi),     \\ L_-[-\bar{c}\Psi+c\bar{\Psi}]  &=&    4i( b_0- \alpha_0 \varphi_0) +
 \\
 \nonumber
 &+& 2 i h[ V\varphi_0\Im[c\bar{d}]+V \Im[c\bar{\Psi}] - \alpha_0 \varphi_0\Re[c \bar{d}]-\alpha_0 \Re[c\bar{\Psi}]]+ h^2 E_2,
  \end{eqnarray}
  where $E_1,E_2$ are smooth functions of the respective arguments.
 This is the system that we need to solve - that is, the goal is to find a neighborhood $(0,h_0)$, so that for every $h\in (0,h_0)$, there is a scalar function $d=d(h)$ and a function $\Psi=\Psi(h)\in \{\varphi_0\}^\perp$, so that the pair satisfies the previous two relations.

 To that end, we shall use the implicit function theorem.  It is clear that it is more convenient to introduce two real  variables\footnote{recall that $c$ is already fixed in terms of $\alpha_0$, so finding $D_1, D_2$ is akin to finding the complex number  $d$} $D_1:=\Re[c\bar{d}], D_2:=\Im[c\bar{d}]$. Clearly, the system requires some solvability conditions. We have already established that with our choice of $c$, we have that $c-\bar{c} -i(c+\bar{c})-4 i \alpha_0 \varphi_0\perp \varphi_0$. So, from \eqref{317},  we need to require
 \begin{eqnarray*}
 	0 &=& \dpr{V\varphi_0\Im(c\bar{d})+V \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]- \alpha_0 \varphi_0\Re[c \bar{d}]-\alpha_0 \Re [c\bar{\Psi}]}{\varphi_0}+O(h)= \\
 	&=&
 	\dpr{D_2 V\varphi_0 - D_1 \alpha_0 \varphi_0 + V \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]}{\varphi_0}+O(h)
 \end{eqnarray*}
 In the last identity, we used that    $\Psi\perp \varphi_0$, whence  by the reality of $\varphi_0$, we have that $\bar{\Psi}\perp \varphi_0$ as well (and thus  any linear combination of $\Psi, \bar{\Psi}$ is perpendicular to $\varphi_0$).  Thus, we end up requiring
 \begin{equation} \dpr{D_2 V\varphi_0 - D_1 \alpha_0 \varphi_0 + V \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]}{\varphi_0}+O(h)=0
 \end{equation}
 Since  $\bar{c}\Psi+c\bar{\Psi}\perp \varphi_0$  ,  we need to have
$$
 0=4 a_0 \dpr{L_+^{-1}[1]}{\varphi_0} +8  D_1 \dpr{L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0^3]}{1}+O(h).
 $$
 Recalling that $\dpr{L_+^{-1}[1]}{\varphi_0}=0$ and   $L_+[\varphi_0]=-4\varphi_0^3$,  whence  $L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0^3]=-\f{1}{4}\varphi_0$ and the previous relation reads
 \begin{equation} -2D_1 \dpr{\varphi_0}{1} +O(h)=0.
 \end{equation}
 The analysis so far allows us to solve the system\eqref{315}, \eqref{317}, for $h=0$.   Namely,  from \eqref{330}, we infer  that
 \begin{equation} D_1^0=0
 \end{equation}
 The next step is to find $\Psi^0$, from \eqref{315}and \eqref{317}, at $h=0$. Inverting   $L_+$ in \eqref{315} and $L_-$ in \eqref{317} and taking the difference,  and taking into account that $\Re[c\bar{d}]=D_1^0+O(h)=O(h)$, we obtain\footnote{Recall that  $b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0\perp \varphi_0$, so taking $L_-^{-1}$  is justified. Similarly, with the definition of $D_1^0$ in \eqref{340}, taking $L_+^{-1}$ is justified as well.}
  \begin{equation} \Psi^0 =  \f{4 a_0  L_+^{-1}[1]- 4 i L_-^{-1}[ b_0 - \alpha_0 \varphi_0]}{2\bar{c}}= c a_0 L_+^{-1}[1] - i c L_-^{-1}[ b_0 - \alpha_0\varphi_0].
 \end{equation}
 Note that $\Psi^0\perp \varphi_0$ (as it should be), since $L_+^{-1}[1]\perp \varphi_0$, and
 $Image[ L_-^{-1}]\perp \varphi_0$.


  Finally, we use \eqref{320} to determine $D_2^0$. We obtain the formula
 \begin{equation} D_2^0\dpr{V^0 \varphi_0}{\varphi_0}=-\dpr{\Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]}{V^0 \varphi_0}.
 \end{equation}
  We clearly need to compute $\Re[c\bar{\Psi}_0], \Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]$. We have from \eqref{350},
  \begin{eqnarray*}
\Re[c\bar{\Psi}_0] &=&    2 a_0  L_+^{-1}[1],      \\
\Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]&=&  2 L_-^{-1}[b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0].
  \end{eqnarray*}
  According to its definition
  $$
  V^0=V(0, \Psi_0)=2  \varphi_0^2 D_1^0+\varphi_0[c \bar{\Psi^0}+\bar{c}\Psi^0]=2\varphi_0\Re[c\bar{\Psi}_0]=
  2 a_0  \varphi_0 L_+^{-1}[1].
  $$
  Consequently, since $L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0^3]=-\f{1}{4} \varphi_0$,
   \begin{equation} \dpr{V^0 \varphi_0}{\varphi_0} = 4 a_0  \dpr{\varphi_0^3}{L_+^{-1}[1]}= - a_0  \dpr{1}{\varphi_0}.
   \end{equation}
   Finally,
     \begin{eqnarray*}
   \dpr{\Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]}{V^0 \varphi_0} = 8 a_0 \dpr{\varphi_0^2 L_+^{-1}[1]}{L_-^{-1}[b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0]}.
      \end{eqnarray*}
      From \eqref{c:14}, we deduce
      \begin{equation} D_2^0=  8 \f{\dpr{\varphi_0^2 L_+^{-1}[1]}{L_-^{-1}[b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0]}}{\dpr{1}{\varphi_0}}
      \end{equation}



 To recapitulate, we have determined, in  \eqref{350}, together with $D_1^0, D_2^0$ as determined above,
 the unique solutions of \eqref{315} and \eqref{317}, when $h=0$.
 We now setup the implicit function argument, which will work in a neighborhood of the solution $h=0$, $\Psi^0$, given by \eqref{350}, and $ D_1^0, D_2^0$.






 First, we set the solvability condition arising in \eqref{317}, namely the scalar function\footnote{Here we use again that $\dpr{ \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]}{\varphi_0}=0$}
 \begin{eqnarray*}
& & Q_1(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2) = 2i\dpr{D_2  V(D_1, \Psi)\varphi_0 +V \Im[c\bar{\Psi}] - \alpha_0 \varphi_0 D_1 -\alpha_0 \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]}{\varphi_0}+ \\
&+& h \dpr{E_2(h,\Psi, D_1, D_2)}{\varphi_0}  = 2i\dpr{D_2  V(D_1, \Psi)\varphi_0 + V(D_1, \Psi) \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]  - \alpha_0 \varphi_0D_1 }{\varphi_0}+\\
&+& h \dpr{E_2(h,\Psi, D_1, D_2)}{\varphi_0},
 \end{eqnarray*}
 where $V(D_1, \Psi)=2 D_1 \varphi_0^2 + \varphi_0(\bar{c} \Psi+c \bar{\Psi})$. The other function is constructed as follows - apply $L_+^{-1}$ in \eqref{315} and $L_-^{-1}$ in \eqref{317} (once we make  sure that the right hand side is orthogonal to $\varphi_0$).  After subtracting and simplifying,
 \begin{eqnarray*}
& & Q_2(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2) =  2 \bar{c} \Psi -\left[ 4 a_0 L_+^{-1}[1] - 2  D_1 \varphi_0    +h L_+^{-1}[E_1(h; \Psi, D_1,D_2)]  \right]
+4i L_-^{-1}[b_0 -  \alpha_0 \varphi_0] \\
& & + L_-^{-1}[P_{\{\varphi_0\}^\perp}[2 i h(D_2 V(D_1, \Psi) \varphi_0 -D_1 \alpha_0\varphi_0+V(D_1, \Psi) \Im[c\bar{\Psi}]-\alpha_0 \Im[c\bar{\Psi}])+h^2 E_2(h; \Psi, D_1,D_2) ]].
 \end{eqnarray*}
 Note that the projection $P_{\{\varphi_0\}^\perp}$ becomes irrelevant, once we impose the condition \\
 $Q_1(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2)=0$! On the other hand, we need it in the definition of $Q_2$ to keep it well-defined, even when $Q_1(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2)=0$ is not enforced. We now consider
 $$
 (Q_1, Q_2)(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2): \mathbf R\times \{\varphi_0\}^\perp \times \mathbf R\times \mathbf R \to \mathbf R\times L^2_{per.}[-T,T]
 $$
 and we would like to solve
\begin{equation} \left|
 \begin{array}{c}
 Q_1(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2)=0 \\
 Q_2(h; \Psi, D_1, D_2)=0.
 \end{array}
 \right.
\end{equation}
 Note that if one obtains solutions to \eqref{485}, the projection $P_{\{\varphi_0\}^\perp}$ becomes irrelevant and the system  $Q_1=Q_2=0$ becomes equivalent to the system \eqref{315}and \eqref{317}.
 Observe that by our earlier considerations, for $h=0$, we have a solution, that is
 $$
 \left|
 \begin{array}{c}
 Q_1(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)=0 \\
 Q_2(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)=0,
 \end{array}
 \right.
 $$
 where $Q_2^0$ is given in \eqref{c:17}.
 Our construction of the family $\Psi(h), D_1(h), D_2(h)$ in a neighborhood $(0,h_0)$ will follow, once we can verify that
 $$
 d(Q_1, Q_2)(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\cdot, \cdot, \cdot]:  \{\varphi_0\}^\perp \times \mathbf R\times \mathbf R \to \mathbf R\times L^2_{per.}[-T,T]
 $$
 is an isomorphism. That is, for every $\chi\in L^2_{per.}[-T,T]$ and $z\in \mathbf R$, there must
 be unique solution $\psi\in \{\varphi_0\}^\perp, d_1 \in \mathbf R, d_2\in \mathbf R$  of the linear system
 \begin{eqnarray*}
 & & dQ_1(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]=z \\
 & & dQ_2(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]=\chi
 \end{eqnarray*}
 so that the linear mapping $(\chi, z)\to (\psi(\chi, z), d_1(\chi, z), d_2(\chi, z))$ is continuous.

 First, we compute $dQ_2(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]= 2\bar{c} \psi + 2 d_1 \varphi_0$.
 In order to prepare the calculation for $ dQ_1(0; \Psi^0,0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]$, observe that
 \begin{eqnarray*}
V(D_1, \Psi) &=& 2 D_1 \varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0 \Re[c\bar{\Psi}] \\
dV(0,\Psi^0)(d_1, \psi)  &=& 2 d_1 \varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0 \Re[c\bar{\psi}]
 \end{eqnarray*}
 Consequently,
  \begin{eqnarray*}
  	 & & dQ_1(0; \Psi^0,0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2] =  2i\dpr{d_2 V^0\varphi_0+ D_2^0(2 d_1\varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0\Re[c\bar{\psi}])}{\varphi_0}+ \\
  	 &+& 2i\dpr{(2 d_1 \varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0\Re[c\bar{\psi}]) \Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]}{\varphi_0} +2i \dpr{V^0 \Im[c\bar{\psi}]}{\varphi_0} - 2i \alpha_0 d_1 \|\varphi_0\|^2.
  \end{eqnarray*}
 Now, the equation $\chi=dQ_2(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]$, has the form
 \begin{eqnarray*}

 & &\chi=  dQ_2(0; \Psi^0, 0, D_2^0)[\psi, d_1, d_2]= 2\bar{c} \psi + 2 d_1 \varphi_0.
 \end{eqnarray*}
  It clearly has the unique solution
  $$
  d_1=\f{\dpr{\chi}{\varphi_0}}{2\|\varphi_0\|^2}, \psi=\f{1}{2\bar{c}}(\chi- 2d_1 \varphi_0)\in \{\varphi_0\}^\perp
  $$
   Plugging the expressions for $d_1$ and $\psi$ in the   equation $dQ_1=z$  produces a linear equation for $d_2$, once we take a dot product with $\varphi_0$.  More precisely,
   \begin{eqnarray*}
  d_2 \dpr{V^0\varphi_0}{\varphi_0} &=&   \f{z}{2i} -\dpr{D_2^0(2 d_1\varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0\Re[c\bar{\psi}])}{\varphi_0} -  \dpr{(2 d_1 \varphi_0^2+2\varphi_0\Re[c\bar{\psi}]) \Im[c\bar{\Psi}_0]}{\varphi_0} +\\
  &+& \alpha_0 d_1 \|\varphi_0\|^2 - \dpr{V^0 \Im[c\bar{\psi}]}{\varphi_0}
   \end{eqnarray*}
   which has also unique solution, provided the coefficient in front of it, $\dpr{V^0 \varphi_0}{\varphi_0}\neq 0$  is non-zero. But we have already verfied that, see \eqref{c:27}. We also see that the solution $d_2$ depends linearly,  through a nice formula on $\chi, z$. It follows that the mapping $(\chi, z)\to (\psi, d_1, d_2)$ is indeed an isomorphism, in the sense specified above.  The implicit function theorem thus applies and we have constructed the solutions.

   It remains to verify the  formulas \eqref{500}and \eqref{510}. First, we have that $c\bar{d}=D_1^0+i D_2^0+O(h)=i D_2^0+O(h)$, whence
\begin{equation} d^0= - \f{i c}{2} D_2^0=\f{a_0+b_0}{2} D_2^0 +i\f{b_0-a_0}{2} D_2^0.
\end{equation}
   Thus, starting with the relation $\varphi_{\alpha,1}-\varphi_{\alpha,2}+i (\varphi_{\alpha,1}-\varphi_{\alpha,2})=q=(c+d h)\varphi_0 +h \Psi$, we deduce
    \begin{eqnarray*}
     \varphi_{\alpha,1} &=& (a_0+\f{b_0}{2} h D_2^0)\varphi_0 +h(a_0^2 L_+^{-1}[1]+b_0 L_-^{-1}[b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0]) +O(h^2)\\
     \varphi_{\alpha,2} &=&(b_0-\f{a_0}{2} h D_2^0)\varphi_0 +h(a_0 b_0 L_+^{-1}[1]-a_0 L_-^{-1}[b_0-\alpha_0 \varphi_0]) +O(h^2),
    \end{eqnarray*}
 which is the final claim in Theorem \ref{102}.
nodes.statement_short: Lyapunov-Schmidt type reduction: write $q=(c+dh)\varphi_0+h\Psi$, solve the $h=0$ problem explicitly and apply the implicit function theorem. Key step: the linearization at $h=0$ is an isomorphism since $\langle V^0\varphi_0,\varphi_0\rangle\neq0$.

  is a real-valued function as

nodes.name: Solvability from (315)
nodes.statement:
Since  $\bar{c}\Psi+c\bar{\Psi}\perp \varphi_0$  ,  we need to have
$$

nodes.name: Stability as Re mu <= alpha
nodes.statement:
{\it Our task here is a bit unusual in that we need to make a good distinction between \eqref{540} and \eqref{550}}.  More precisely, our goal is to find conditions (or actually characterize) the waves that are stable, or equivalently we need to ensure that the eigenvalue problem \eqref{540}, $\lambda$, satisfy $\Re \lambda\leq 0$.  In terms of $\mu$, the stability is equivalent to $\Re\mu\leq \alpha$.
 Here and below, we use the instability index theory developed for eigenvalue problems in the form \eqref{550}, which among other things counts eigenvalues with positive real parts for \eqref{550}. Let us reiterate again, that the existence of those does not necessarily mean instability for \eqref{540}, unless $\Re\mu>\alpha=\alpha_0 h$. In fact, we have already one ``instability'' for \eqref{550}, namely an eigenvalue $\mu=\alpha$, with e-vector $\left(\begin{array}{c} \varphi_{\alpha,1}' \\ \varphi_{\alpha,2}'\end{array} \right)$.

nodes.name: Ansatz

nodes.name: Leading-order equations
nodes.statement_short: Collect order-$h$ terms.

nodes.name: Solvability gives sigma_0
nodes.statement_short: The solvability condition yields $\sigma_0$.

nodes.name: Plug in

nodes.name: Solve for q_1
nodes.statement:
Resolving the first equation, to its leading order $\sqrt{h}$,  yields the relation
$
L_+ q_1 = -\mu_0 \varphi_0,
$
or, since $L_+$ is invertible on $\varphi_0$,
\begin{equation} q_1=-\mu_0 L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0]+O(\sqrt{h}).
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Solve for q_2
nodes.statement:
In the second equation, the leading order is $h$, whence we get the equation
\begin{equation} L_- q_2 - 4  \varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0) = \mu_0 q_1= -\mu_0^2  L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0].
\end{equation}
This equation is solvable, provided we ensure $4  \varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0)  - \mu_0^2  L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0]\perp \varphi_0$, as the operator $L_-$ becomes invertible on it, whence
$$
q_2=L_-^{-1}[4  \varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0)  - \mu_0^2  L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0]].
$$
nodes.statement_short: Solvability of the $L_-$ equation.

nodes.statement:

where $\mu_0$ ensures $4  \varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0)  - \mu_0^2  L_+^{-1}[\varphi_0]\perp \varphi_0$.
Equivalently
\begin{equation} \mu_0^2 = 4 \f{\dpr{\varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0 \Psi_2^0)}{\varphi_0}}{\dpr{L_+^{-1}\varphi_0}{\varphi_0}}.
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Sign dichotomy
nodes.statement:
Since $\dpr{L_+^{-1}\varphi_0}{\varphi_0}<0$, we have that $sgn(\mu_0^2)=sgn(a_0)$. In other words, if $a_0>0$, we have instability, while for $a_0<0$, we have a marginally stable pairs of eigenvalues
$\pm i [\sqrt  \f{-a_0 \dpr{\varphi_0}{1}}{\dpr{L_+^{-1}\varphi_0}{\varphi_0}} \sqrt{h}+O(h)]$
nodes.statement_short: $a_0>0$ gives instability, $a_0<0$ a marginally stable pair.

nodes.name: Putting it together
nodes.statement:
Before we proceed with our rigorous arguments, let us discuss our findings so far. In the case
$a_0>0$ (or equivalently $\sigma_0>0$), we have an unstable eigenvalue in the form $\mu_0 \sqrt{h}+O(h)$, where $\mu_0$ is real and
determined from \eqref{610}. The case where $\mu_0$ is purely imaginary
 is more complicated and it needs extra arguments, based on our earlier computations of the sign of the eigenvalues and the index theory.

 Henceforth,  assume $a_0<0$. Also, it is clear that both the even and odd subspaces are invariant under the action of ${\mathcal L}_h$ and ${\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h$, so we will consider them separately.
 \subsubsection{Spectral analysis on the even subspace}  In this case, we have established the emergence,
  from the modulational eigenvalue at $h=0$ (which has algebraic multiplicity two!),  of  a pair of marginally stable eigenvalues
  $i [\pm \mu_0  \sqrt{h}+O(h)]$.
  We now compute the Krein index of  the marginally stable pair  of eigenvalues\footnote{which is of course relevant computation, only if $b_0>a_0$.} $ \pm i \sqrt{\mu_0} \sqrt{h} +O(h)$    For a simple pair of eigenvalues, the Krein index coincides with the sign of the expression
  $\dpr{  \Re \left(\begin{array}{c}
  \sqrt{h} q_1  \\ \varphi_0+h q_2
  \end{array}\right)}{ \mathcal M_h \Re \left(\begin{array}{c}
  	\sqrt{h} q_1  \\ \varphi_0+h q_2
  	\end{array}\right)}$, see \cite{KKS}, p. 267. To this end,  realizing from \eqref{598} that $q_1$ is purely imaginary to the leading order (in the case under consideration),
  \begin{eqnarray*}
  & &  \dpr{  \Re \left(\begin{array}{c}
   		\sqrt{h} q_1  \\ \varphi_0+h q_2
   	\end{array}\right)}{ \mathcal M_h \Re \left(\begin{array}{c}
   	\sqrt{h} q_1  \\ \varphi_0+h q_2
   \end{array}\right)}  =   -4h \dpr{\varphi_0}{\varphi_0^2(a_0 \Psi_1^0+b_0\Psi_2^0)}+O(h^{3/2})= \\
  &=&
-4 a_0 h \dpr{\varphi_0^3}{L_+^{-1}[1]}+O(h^{3/2})= a_0 h  \dpr{\varphi_0}{1}+O(h^{3/2}).
\end{eqnarray*}
  It follows that for $a_0<0$,  the problem has a pair of eigenvalues $ \pm i \sqrt{\mu_0} \sqrt{h} +O(h)$  with a negative Krein signature.





  Recall that $n({\mathcal L}_0)=1$, which arises in the even subspace.  Moreover, $dim(Ker[{\mathcal L}_0])=2$, but recall that one of them occurs in the even subspace, the other one in the odd subspace. On the other hand\footnote{For a self-adjoint, bounded from below operator $M$, acting invariantly on the even subspace, we denote $n_{even}(M)$ the number of negative eigenvalues, when acting on the even subspace}
  $n_{even}({\mathcal L}_h)$ could assume the values of
 one  or two - $n_{even}({\mathcal L}_h)=1$,   if the translational eigenvalue \eqref{b:50} is positive or  $n_{even}({\mathcal L}_h)=2$, if the   modulational eigenvalue \eqref{b:50} is negative. Indeed, ${\mathcal L}_{0, even}$ has one negative eigenvalue, according to Proposition \ref{prop:h0} - which remains negative, after the perturbation. In addition, the modulational eigenvalue at zero has moved (for $a_0<0$) to the left, see \eqref{b:90}, creating a second negative eigenvalue.

  We claim that
 $n({\mathcal L}_h)=2$, at least for small $0<h<<1$.  Indeed, since by the index counting formulas
 $$
   0\leq n_{unstable, even}({\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h)\leq n({\mathcal L}_h)-\# \{\lambda\in i \mathbf R: \lambda \ \ \textup{has negative Krein signature}  \}\leq
 n_{even}({\mathcal L}_h)-2\leq 0.
  $$
since we have already verified that there is at least one  pair of purely imaginary eigenvalues, $\pm i \sqrt{\mu_0} \sqrt{h} +O(h)$  with negative Krein signatures (and even eigenfunctions!). Thus, we obtain equalities everywhere in the inequalities above, in particular $n_{unstable, even }({\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h)=0$, \\ $n({\mathcal L}_{h, even})=2$.


In other words,      the  modulational  eigenvalue has moved to the left (for $a_0<0$), creating  a total of
two negative eigenvalue for ${\mathcal L}_h$  - one that existed for ${\mathcal L}_0$ (and it is still there, after the perturbation), to which another one is added.  These  are subsequently offset by two purely imaginary eigenvalues, with negative Krein signatures.


\subsubsection{Spectral analysis on the odd subspace}

For the odd subspace, the index count is somewhat simpler.
Recall  there is the ``unstable'' eigenvalue at $\mu=\alpha=\alpha_0 h$ for the eigenvalue problem \eqref{570}, which
corresponds to the translational invariance,  see \eqref{550} and the discussion immediately after. So, this implies that $n_{unstable, odd}({\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h)\geq 1$. On the other hand, $n_{odd}(L_+)\leq 1$, since the translational eigenvalue has moved either to the left (in which case $n_{odd}(L_+)=1$), or to the right, and then\footnote{See the Appendix for a calculation involving the direction of the move, which turns out to be  inconclusive to first order}  $n_{odd}(L_+)=0$. Applying the index counting theory, we have that on the other hand $n_{odd}(L_+)\geq n_{unstable,odd}({\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h)$, whence $1=n_{unstable, odd}({\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h)=n_{odd}(L_+)$. In particular, the translational eigenvalue has moved to the left to become a negative eigenvalue  for ${\mathcal L}_{+,h}$. In addition, the ``unstable eigenvalue'' is exactly the one computed explicitly, namely $\mu=\alpha$ and there are no other unstable eigenvalues in the odd subspace. Note that by the Hamiltonian symmetry the eigenvalues of \eqref{570}are symmetric with respect to the imaginary axes, so there is another, stable  one at $\mu=-\alpha$. We mention that there could be (and there is!) a lot of (point) spectrum on the imaginary axes as well.

In terms of the  original spectral
variables, by combining the conclusions for the even and odd subspaces, we obtain
$$
\lambda=\mu-\alpha\subset \left\{\{\alpha\}\cup\{-\alpha\} \cup \{\lambda: \Re \lambda=0\} \right\} - \alpha =   \{0\}\cup\{-2\alpha\} \cup \{\lambda: \Re \lambda=-\alpha\}.
$$
  This is exactly the statement of Theorem  \ref{105} and the proof is completed.

Applying the index counting theory, we have that on the other hand $n_{odd}(L_+)\geq n_{unstable,odd}({\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h)$, whence $1=n_{unstable, odd}({\mathcal J} {\mathcal L}_h)=n_{odd}(L_+)$. In particular, the translational eigenvalue has moved to the left to become a negative eigenvalue  for ${\mathcal L}_{+,h}$.
nodes.statement_short: Index counting gives exactly one odd unstable eigenvalue.

nodes.name: Hamiltonian symmetry
nodes.statement: In addition, the ``unstable eigenvalue'' is exactly the one computed explicitly, namely $\mu=\alpha$ and there are no other unstable eigenvalues in the odd subspace. Note that by the Hamiltonian symmetry the eigenvalues of \eqref{570}are symmetric with respect to the imaginary axes, so there is another, stable  one at $\mu=-\alpha$. We mention that there could be (and there is!) a lot of (point) spectrum on the imaginary axes as well.
nodes.statement_short: It is $\mu=\alpha$; its mirror is $\mu=-\alpha$.

nodes.name: Back to lambda
nodes.statement:
In terms of the  original spectral
variables, by combining the conclusions for the even and odd subspaces, we obtain
$$
\lambda=\mu-\alpha\subset \left\{\{\alpha\}\cup\{-\alpha\} \cup \{\lambda: \Re \lambda=0\} \right\} - \alpha =   \{0\}\cup\{-2\alpha\} \cup \{\lambda: \Re \lambda=-\alpha\}.
$$
  This is exactly the statement of Theorem  \ref{105} and the proof is completed.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7
nodes.statement:
For the proof of \eqref{ant1},  recall the basic properties at $h=0$. In this case the equation (\ref{1.2}) has a solution
$$\varphi_0(x)=\alpha dn (\alpha x, \kappa), $$
where $\kappa^2=\frac{2\alpha^2-1}{\alpha^2}$. Also $L_+=-\partial_x^2+1-2(\varphi_0)^2$. Since $L_+\varphi_0'=0$,  the function
      $$\psi(x)=\varphi_0'(x)\int^{x}{\frac{1}{\varphi_0'^2(s)}}ds, \; \; \left| \begin{array}{cc} \varphi_0'& \psi \\ \varphi_0'' & \psi'\end{array}\right|=1 $$
      is also solution of $L_+\psi=0$.
      Formally, since $\varphi_0'$ has   zeros  using the identities
        $$\frac{1}{cn^2(y,\kappa)}=\frac{1}{dn(y, \kappa)}\frac{\partial}{\partial_y}\frac{sn(x, \kappa)}{cn(y, \kappa)}, \; \;
        \frac{1}{sn^2(y,\kappa)}=-\frac{1}{dn(y, \kappa)}\frac{\partial}{\partial_y}\frac{cn(x, \kappa)}{sn(y, \kappa)}$$
        and integrating by parts we get
       $$
        \psi(x) =\frac{1}{\alpha^2\kappa^2}\left[\frac{1-2sn^2(\alpha x, \kappa )}{dn (\alpha x, \kappa) }
        - \alpha \kappa^2sn(\alpha x, \kappa)cn(\alpha x, \kappa)  \int_{0}^{x}{\frac{1-2sn^2(\alpha s, \kappa )}{dn^2(\alpha s, \kappa)}}ds\right]
       $$
       Thus, we may construct Green function
         $$L_+^{-1}f=\varphi_0'\int_{0}^{x}{\psi(s)f(s)}ds-\psi(s)\int_{0}^{x}{\varphi_0'(s)f(s)}s+C_f\psi(x), $$
         where $C_f$ is chosen such that $L_{+,0}^{-1}f$ is periodic with same period as $\varphi_0(x)$.
         After integrating by parts, we get
           \begin{equation} \langle L_+^{-1}\varphi_0, \varphi_0\rangle = -\langle \varphi_0^3, \psi \rangle +\frac{\varphi_0^2(T)+\varphi_0^2}{2}\langle \varphi_0, \psi \rangle +C_{\varphi_0}\langle \varphi_0, \psi \rangle,
           \end{equation}
   We have
             \begin{equation} \begin{array}{ll}
               \langle \varphi_0, \psi \rangle =\frac{1}{\alpha^2 \kappa^2}[E(\kappa)-K(\kappa)] \\
               \\
               \langle \varphi_0^3, \psi \rangle =\frac{1}{2\kappa^2} [(2-\kappa^2)E(\kappa)-2(1-\kappa^2)K(\kappa)] \\
               \\
               C_{\varphi_0}=-\frac{\varphi_0''(T)}{2\psi(T)}\langle \varphi_0, \psi \rangle+\frac{\varphi_0^2(T)-\varphi_0^2(0)}{2}.
               \end{array}
             \end{equation}
            With this finally we get
             $$\dpr{L_+^{-1} \varphi_0} {\varphi_0} = \frac{E^2(\kappa)-(1-\kappa^2)K^2(\kappa)}{2[2(1-\kappa^2)K(\kappa)-(2-\kappa^2)E(\kappa)]}<0.
             $$
             see Figure \ref{fig1} below.
             \begin{figure}[h]
             	\centering
             	\includegraphics[width=8cm,height=6cm]{grafika_1.pdf}
             	\caption{The function $k\to\frac{E^2(\kappa)-(1-\kappa^2)K^2(\kappa)}{2[2(1-\kappa^2)K(\kappa)-(2-\kappa^2)E(\kappa)]}$ } \end{figure}

              For the proof of \eqref{ant2},  we have
             $$L_+^{-1}[1]=\varphi_0'\int_{0}^{x}\psi (s) ds-\psi (x)\int_{0}^{x}\varphi_0'(s)ds, $$
             and
             $$\dpr{L_+^{-1} [1]} {\varphi_0}=\frac{\varphi_0^2(T)}{2}\int_{-T}^{T}{\psi(x)}dx-\frac{3}{2}\int_{-T}^{T}{\psi(x)\varphi_0^2(x)}dx+[C_1+\varphi_0(0)]\int_{-T}^{T}{\psi(x)\varphi_0(x)}dx,$$
             where$$C_1=\varphi_0(T)-\varphi (0)-\frac{\varphi_0''(T)}{\psi'(T)}\int_{0}^{T}{\psi(x)}dx.$$
             Using that $\frac{d}{dx} dn(x)=-\kappa^2sn(x)cn(x)$ and integrating be parts, we get  
             $$\begin{array}{ll}
             \int_{-T}^{T}{\psi(x)\varphi_0(x)}dx & =\frac{2}{\kappa^2} \left[ \frac{2}{3}\int_{0}^{T}{dn(\alpha x)(1-2sn^2(\alpha x))}dx+\frac{1}{3}dn^3(\alpha T)\int_{0}^{T}{\frac{1-2sn^2(\alpha x)}{dn^2(\alpha x)}}dx\right] \\
             \\
              & =\frac{2}{3\kappa^2}dn^3(K)\int_{0}^{T}{\frac{1-2sn^2(\alpha x)}{dn^2(\alpha x)}}dx.
             \end{array} $$
             Similarly, integrating be parts
               $$\int_{-T}^{T}{\psi(x)}dx=\frac{2dn(\alpha T)}{\alpha^2\kappa^2}\int_{0}^{T}{\frac{1-2sn^2(\alpha x)}{dn^2(\alpha x)}}dx.$$
               Thus,
             $$
             \frac{\varphi_0^2(T)}{2}\int_{-T}^{T}{\psi(x)}dx-\frac{3}{2}\int_{-T}^{T}{\psi(x)\varphi_0^2(x)}dx=0.
             $$
             Using that $\varphi_0''(T)=\alpha^3\kappa^2\sqrt{1-\kappa^2}$, and $\psi'(T)=\sqrt{1-\kappa^2}\int_{0}^{T}{\frac{1-2sn^2(\alpha x)}{dn^2(\alpha x)}}dx$, we get
             $$
             C_1+\varphi_0(0)=\varphi_0(T)-\frac{\varphi_0''(T)}{\psi'(T)}\int_{0}^{T}{\psi(x)}=0.
             $$
             For the proof of \eqref{ant3},
            \begin{eqnarray*}
      \dpr{L_+^{-1} [1]} {\varphi_0(x)(\varphi_0'(x))^2} &=& \int_{-T}^{T}{\varphi_0(x)(\varphi_0'(x))^3\int_{0}^{x}{\psi(s)}ds}dx-
      \int_{-T}^{T}{\psi(x)\varphi_0^2(x)(\varphi_0'(x))^2}dx\\
        	& + & (C_1+\varphi_0(0))\int_{-T}^{T}{\psi(x)\varphi_0(x)(\varphi_0'(x))^2}dx.
            \end{eqnarray*}

             Again integrating by parts, we get 
             $$\int_{0}^{x}{\psi(s)}ds=\frac{dn(\alpha x)}{\alpha^2 \kappa^2}\int_{0}^{x}{\frac{1-2sn^2(\alpha s)}{dn^2(\alpha s)}}ds,$$
              and
             $$
             \begin{array}{ll}
             \int_{-T}^{T}{\varphi_0(x)(\varphi_0'(x))^3\int_{0}^{x}{\psi(s)}ds}dx-\int_{-T}^{T}{\psi(x)\varphi_0^2(x)(\varphi_0'(x))^2}dx\\
             \\
             =\int_{-T}^{T}{\varphi_0(x)(\varphi_0'(x))^2\left[ \varphi_0'(x)\int_{0}^{x}{\psi(s)}ds-\psi(x)\varphi_0(x)\right]}dx \\
             \\
             =-\alpha^3\kappa^2\int_{0}^{K(\kappa)}{(1-2sn^2(x))sn^2(x)cn^2(x)dn(x)}dx=0.
             \end{array} $$

 Now, using that $\kappa^2=\frac{2\alpha^2-1}{\alpha^2}$, we get
               $$
               \begin{array}{ll}
               \int_0^T \f{(2-6\varphi_0^2(y))((\varphi_0'(y))^2-(\varphi_0''(y))^2)}{((\varphi_0'(y))^2+(\varphi_0''(y))^2))^2} dy
               =\int_{0}^{K(\kappa)}{\frac{\left(2-\frac{6}{2-\kappa^2}dn^2(y)\right)\left( sn^2(y)cn^2(y)-\frac{1}{2-\kappa^2}[cn^2(y)-sn^2(y)]^2dn^2(y)\right)}{\left[ sn^2(y)cn^2(y)+\frac{1}{2-\kappa^2}[cn^2(y)-sn^2(y)]^2dn^2(y)\right]^2}}dy.
               \end{array}
               $$
               Using Mathematica, we were able to compute this last expression
               $$
               \int_0^T \f{(2-6\varphi_0^2(y))((\varphi_0'(y))^2-(\varphi_0''(y))^2)}{((\varphi_0'(y))^2+(\varphi_0''(y))^2))^2} dy = 2 K(k) - \f{(2-k^2)}{1-k^2} E(k)<0,
               $$
               as is clear from Figure \ref{fig2} below.
               \begin{figure}[hh]
               	\centering
               	\includegraphics[width=8cm,height=6cm]{grafika_2.pdf}
               	\caption{The function $k \to 2 K(k) - \f{(2-k^2)}{1-k^2} E(k).$ } \end{figure}

             $$\int_{0}^{x}{\psi(s)}ds=\frac{dn(\alpha x)}{\alpha^2 \kappa^2}\int_{0}^{x}{\frac{1-2sn^2(\alpha s)}{dn^2(\alpha s)}}ds,$$

             \begin{array}{ll}
             \int_{-T}^{T}{\varphi_0(x)(\varphi_0'(x))^3\int_{0}^{x}{\psi(s)}ds}dx-\int_{-T}^{T}{\psi(x)\varphi_0^2(x)(\varphi_0'(x))^2}dx\\
             \\
             =\int_{-T}^{T}{\varphi_0(x)(\varphi_0'(x))^2\left[ \varphi_0'(x)\int_{0}^{x}{\psi(s)}ds-\psi(x)\varphi_0(x)\right]}dx \\
             \\
             =-\alpha^3\kappa^2\int_{0}^{K(\kappa)}{(1-2sn^2(x))sn^2(x)cn^2(x)dn(x)}dx=0.
             \end{array} $$
